model.description: Randomized integer factoring: given an integer N >= 2 in binary, with b bits, output its complete factorization into primes. The algorithm can use random bits: independent fair coins, each read at cost one. On every input and every run, the output must be correct, and the algorithm must halt with probability 1 (a Las Vegas algorithm). Time is the expected number of bit operations, in the worst case over all inputs N with b bits (steps of a multitape Turing machine or of a word RAM with O(log b)-bit words: an expected time T on one model gives an expected time T^{O(1)} on the other, and a polynomial in the time does not change theta. The second ranking key, the constant c of L_N[theta, c], uses the multitape Turing machine time, because squaring the time doubles c; a RAM bound converts with its own overhead). One algorithm for all N. Output of only the smallest prime factor gives the same scores (the complete factorization takes at most b such searches, and it contains the smallest prime factor). A deterministic algorithm also qualifies. A bound must be unconditional: a result that assumes an unproved hypothesis does not score. A hypothesis counts as met when this site lists it as a Lean Verified theorem; today, that is the generalized Riemann hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, which Levent Alpöge proved (Lean Verified on the Quasi-Riemann hypothesis board).

score.definition: theta, lower is better. Expected time 2^{(log N)^{theta+o(1)}} = 2^{b^{theta+o(1)}} with 0 <= theta <= 1 scores theta: for every fixed epsilon > 0, the expected time is at most 2^{b^{theta+epsilon}} for all large b. Factors b^{O(1)} do not change a score. A time L_N[a, c] = e^{(c+o(1))(ln N)^a (ln ln N)^{1-a}} with 0 < a < 1 scores theta = a, whatever the constant c > 0 is. Rows with the same theta rank by c, lower is better, with c of the multitape Turing machine time (l_constant; the row shows L_N[theta, c]); a row that states no c ranks after every row that states one. Then rows rank by evidence level, then by date.

keybreak-sjtu-randomized-1-3-2026.credit_note: Joint credit: Kasper Nielsen (kasper0406), whose factoring-connection manuscripts, written with Claude agents, give the multilevel descent weights, the private-root construction, square certification and recursion, and the Riemann hypothesis analysis of the genus-two smoothness test; and the KeyBreak Cryptanalysis Agent of Shanghai Jiao Tong University (harness and prompt by Qi Wang, Zhian Qian, Changhao Yuan, Juanru Li, Xiaogang Zhou, Shi Bai and Yu Yu; base model GPT-6 Astra), which proves the relation-count and incidence estimates for these constructions. The paper says that its descent builds on those manuscripts. The result is expected time \(L_N[1/3, 2.97]\) with the generalized Riemann hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, which Levent Alpöge proved (Lean Verified on our site), and \(L_N[1/3, 1013]\) without it.
